items.title: Pineapples photosynthesise at night
items.claim: Most plants open their stomata in daytime to take in CO2 and lose water to evaporation. CAM plants (crassulacean acid metabolism — cacti, pineapples, agaves) keep stomata SHUT all day and open them only at night, storing CO2 as malic acid for the day's photosynthesis.
items.prompt: Why would a plant fix CO2 in the dark?

options.text: By separating CO2 uptake (cool, humid night) from light reactions (hot, dry day), CAM plants cut water loss by 80-90% versus C3 plants — essential in deserts where transpiration would be lethal

items.reveal:
C3 plants (wheat, rice, ~85% of species): Rubisco fixes CO2 directly in mesophyll cells. Simple, but loses water and suffers photorespiration when hot.

C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sorghum): PEP carboxylase fixes CO2 into a 4-carbon acid (oxaloacetate) in mesophyll cells. The acid is shipped to bundle-sheath cells, where Rubisco operates in a CO2-rich environment. About 3% of species, but include some of the most productive crops.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples, succulents, agaves): same chemistry as C4 but separated in TIME instead of space. Stomata open at night; CO2 is stored as malic acid in vacuoles; daylight releases it for Rubisco.

Each is a different trade-off between water loss, productivity and temperature tolerance. C4 and CAM evolved independently dozens of times — convergent solutions to Rubisco's flaws.
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught as a single process. In reality, plants have invented three biochemically distinct strategies, each suited to a different climate.

items.title: Your body can make antibodies against molecules that don't exist yet
items.claim: Humans have about 20,000 genes. We make perhaps 10 to the 11 different antibody molecules — far more than our genome could encode directly. Including antibodies against viruses we'll never meet.
items.prompt: How do we generate such enormous antibody diversity?

options.text: Each antibody is encoded by a separate gene

V(D)J recombination — during B cell development, gene segments (V, D, J) are randomly chosen and joined with imprecise cuts, and then somatic hypermutation refines the result during an immune response
Antibodies are made up new for each encounter from scratch
The genome reshuffles itself constantly in all cells

items.reveal_title: Tonegawa's discovery — recombination in somatic cells
items.reveal:
Susumu Tonegawa (Nobel 1987) showed that B cells deliberately rearrange their immunoglobulin genes. Each B cell randomly picks one V, one D and one J segment for the heavy chain (V and J for the light chain), joins them with imprecise junctions (adding/deleting nucleotides), and pairs heavy with light. The combinatorial maths gives about 10 to the 11 possible specificities from a few hundred gene segments.

Once a B cell encounters its antigen, somatic hypermutation introduces additional point mutations into the variable region, and selection retains the best binders (affinity maturation).

The result is an immune system that can respond to virtually any molecular shape — including ones never seen before, like artificial drugs.
items.why: Genome size limits direct encoding. The immune system uses combinatorics and somatic mutation to overshoot what the genome alone could specify.

items.title: You synthesise your body weight in ATP every day
items.claim: ATP is the cell's energy currency. Your body contains only about 50 grams at any moment, but you turn it over so fast that you make and consume the equivalent of your full body mass — 60 to 80 kilograms — daily.
items.prompt: How can a tiny pool turn over so much?

options.text: Each ATP molecule is hydrolysed and re-synthesised hundreds of times per day; mitochondria continuously rebuild ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using the proton motive force from respiration
Most of the body's mass is ATP
ATP is consumed only during exercise

items.reveal:
An adult at rest uses about 2000 kcal per day. Each ATP hydrolysis releases ~7.3 kcal/mol of free energy under standard conditions, more under cellular conditions.

Working through: ~65 kg of ATP cycled per day, give or take. Each molecule of ATP cycles roughly 1000-1500 times daily.

The cell stores essentially no ATP for emergencies. It maintains a flux instead. Stop respiration and your ATP pool depletes in seconds — which is exactly why cyanide is so fast.

Muscles store some quick-access energy as phosphocreatine (a few seconds of all-out sprint) and glycogen (~minutes), but ATP itself is continuously regenerated, not stockpiled.

This is metabolism's deep design choice: a small, dynamic currency pool, refilled by continuous oxidation of food.
items.why: Energy storage feels like the obvious solution. Cells went the other way — keep almost no ATP, rebuild it constantly. The flux IS the metabolism.
